comprehensive.reason: Boundary/adapter module — the only file importing @auth0/auth0-spa-js. Profile names it load-bearing for all four axes.
Domain vocabulary (Principal, Session, AuthError) — what app code sees instead of vendor shapes.
Single-flight refresh helper — Axis 2 owned-behavior evidence.
AuthProvider — how the port is injected into the React tree.
API client — the 401 interceptor / owned-refresh path.
App-layer consumer of the port; leak-check target.
App-layer consumer using the policy layer; leak-check target.
App-layer page consuming the domain Principal; leak-check target.
Contract suite — B3 evidence, exercised against both FakeAuth and the real adapter.
Vendor detection — established @auth0/auth0-spa-js v2 was the only auth SDK present.

findings.statement: An AuthPort interface defines the boundary contract in domain terms (methods return Principal / headers / booleans / void), so no vendor shape is required to consume auth.
Domain types (Principal, Session, AuthError) are defined outside any vendor namespace and used everywhere in app code.
The @auth0/auth0-spa-js import — and every Auth0 vendor type — is confined to a single adapter file (src/auth/adapters/auth0.ts); nothing else in src/ imports the SDK.
No Auth0 vendor types (Auth0Client, ICache, User, Auth0ContextInterface, GetTokenSilentlyOptions, AppState, IdToken) appear in app-layer code (components, pages, api client, context, policy).
findings.note: Every vendor-type occurrence in the codebase is inside src/auth/adapters/auth0.ts (adapter) or the vi.mock('@auth0/auth0-spa-js') block in the contract test — both correct.

findings.statement: AuthProvider injects an AuthPort into a React context; components call useAuth() and receive the port + principal without knowing the vendor.
The API client factory receives the AuthPort as a parameter — auth is injected, never imported from the vendor at the call site.

A runAuthContractTests suite asserts against the AuthPort/Principal domain shape and is executed against both an in-memory FakeAuth and the real Auth0 adapter (with the SDK mocked at the import boundary); assertions are vendor-free.
This is a pure SPA; no server-side entry points, no @auth0/nextjs-auth0, no execution-context branching in app code — the client/server split does not arise.
findings.note: The only typeof window check in the tree is inside the adapter's signOut (returnTo: window.location.origin) — a defensive check inside the boundary, not app-code branching to obtain auth.

findings.statement: Token storage uses a custom ICache implementation (MemoryCache) passed via the cache option to createAuth0Client — the real Auth0 storage seam (not the cacheLocation built-in selector).
findings.note: cacheLocation is not set anywhere; the storage decision is fully expressed by the custom cache implementation. Swapping to an HttpOnly-cookie-backed or encrypted store is a single-file change (the MemoryCache class).

findings.statement: A single-flight refresh helper (refreshOnce) collapses concurrent refresh attempts into one in-flight call and clears itself on completion.

The API client owns the 401 path: on 401 it calls auth.onRefresh(), retries once, and on continued failure calls auth.onSessionExpired() — an explicit, owned failure route rather than inherited vendor magic.
The adapter's onRefresh wraps getAccessTokenSilently({ cacheMode: 'off', ... }) inside refreshOnce — a bare vendor refresh call is never used from app code.
findings.note: cacheMode: 'off' forces the SDK to hit the refresh-token flow (useRefreshTokens: true is configured at client creation) rather than serving a still-valid cached token, so onRefresh actually rotates tokens rather than being a no-op.

findings.statement: Auth0-specific configuration (audience, scope, useRefreshTokens, ICache) and API calls (createAuth0Client, getAccessTokenSilently, client.logout) are contained inside src/auth/adapters/auth0.ts.

Auth0 namespaced-claim URL keys (${namespace}roles, ${namespace}tenantId) are read only inside the adapter's getPrincipal; the domain Principal exposes the concept-level names roles / tenantId instead.
No inline namespaced-claim reads (`user['https://.../roles' | permissions | tenantId]`) or bare getAccessTokenSilently calls appear in app-layer code.
A domain policy layer (can(principal, action)) mediates authorization decisions; components call the policy instead of reading Principal.roles inline.

evidence.quote: export function can(principal: Principal | null, action: Action): boolean {

findings.statement: Outbound requests carry the access token obtained via getAccessTokenSilently with an audience configured — a real JWT API access token, not the ID token and not the opaque-token Auth0 anti-pattern.
findings.note: The Auth0 profile explicitly names the misuse signal: a missing `audience` yields an opaque (non-JWT) token or forces the app to lean on the ID token for API auth. This adapter avoids both by requiring `audience` on the options type and passing it through on every getAccessTokenSilently call.

findings.statement: The adapter maps Auth0's user object to the domain Principal (userId / email / tenantId / roles); app code never sees vendor-shaped user objects.

b1_anti_corruption.note: Domain vocabulary in place; vendor types (Auth0Client, ICache) confined to the adapter.

b2_injected.note: AuthPort is passed as a dependency (context, factory param) — never imported from the vendor at a call site.

b3_contract_tested.note: The same runAuthContractTests suite runs against FakeAuth and the real Auth0 adapter with the SDK mocked at the import boundary; assertions test the domain shape.

b4_client_server_split.note: Pure SPA — no SSR entry points exist, so there is no client/server split to absorb. The single typeof window check in the adapter's signOut is defensive code inside the boundary, not app-layer branching.

auth0.note: MemoryCache implements ICache and is passed as the cache option to createAuth0Client. This is the real Auth0 storage seam — not the cacheLocation built-in selector (which the adapter comment explicitly calls out as the look-alike trap). Note: MemoryCache is an in-memory implementation; if the maintainer's target storage is HttpOnly cookies or an encrypted store, the seam is present but the destination implementation is not yet written.

storage.recommended_seam: Keep the ICache abstraction and swap MemoryCache for a concrete implementation matching the target storage (HttpOnly-cookie-backed, encrypted-store, or session-cookie ICache). No app code changes.

cost_evidence.basis: The seam exists in one file (src/auth/adapters/auth0.ts). Zero confirmed call sites in app code touch storage. A storage change is one class replacement inside the adapter; no components, pages, or the API client need to move.

auth0.note: All three ownership signals are present: 401 interceptor (src/api/client.ts), single-flight collapsing (src/auth/refresh.ts), and explicit failure path (auth.onSessionExpired). The adapter's onRefresh uses cacheMode: 'off' with useRefreshTokens: true so refresh actually rotates the token.

refresh.recommended_seam: Already in place: interceptor-owned 401 → onRefresh (single-flight) → onSessionExpired. No refactor recommended.

cost_evidence.basis: Owned refresh is fully in place across three files (client.ts, refresh.ts, adapter). No app code holds a bare vendor refresh call. Changing the refresh mechanism (e.g., moving to server-side refresh via HttpOnly cookies) touches the adapter's onRefresh body only.

auth0.note: Every Auth0-specific surface (createAuth0Client, audience, scope, useRefreshTokens, namespaced-claim URL keys, client.logout logoutParams) is inside src/auth/adapters/auth0.ts. Components and pages import only from ../auth/context and ../auth/policy.

identity_provider.recommended_seam: The adapter file is already the seam. A provider swap = write a sibling adapter (e.g., src/auth/adapters/<new-vendor>.ts) that satisfies AuthPort and pass it through AuthProvider; the same contract suite green-lights the swap.

cost_evidence.basis: Zero confirmed vendor-surface call sites outside src/auth/adapters/auth0.ts. Components, pages, and the api client are provider-agnostic and would not need to change on an adapter swap. The contract suite makes 'migration complete' mechanically checkable — the new adapter must simply make runAuthContractTests green.

auth0.note: Authorization goes through can(principal, action). Namespaced-claim URL keys are read only in getPrincipal and mapped to the domain Principal. The outbound Authorization header carries the access token from getAccessTokenSilently({ authorizationParams: { audience, scope } }) — audience is required by the adapter's options type, so the opaque-token / ID-token-for-API anti-patterns are structurally avoided.

authorization.recommended_seam: Already in place: adapter → domain Principal → policy.can. To evolve the model (e.g., action-scoped permissions), extend the Principal + policy without changing components.

cost_evidence.basis: One policy file (src/auth/policy.ts) mediates all authorization decisions. Two confirmed policy call sites in components; both go through can(). The token-type decision (access token, with audience) is expressed by the adapter's options type — the anti-pattern is not reachable without changing the adapter's public shape.

judgment_calls.question: Is a token storage change actually on the table (e.g., moving MemoryCache to an HttpOnly-cookie-backed or encrypted ICache), or is in-memory acceptable for now?
judgment_calls.context: The custom ICache seam exists and is exercised — swapping the implementation is a single-file change — but MemoryCache itself is a fixture-grade in-memory store. Whether that counts as a 'todo' or 'done' depends on the intended production storage posture, which isn't in the code.

judgment_calls.question: Any owned-refresh change planned beyond what's already here (e.g., server-side refresh via HttpOnly cookies)?
judgment_calls.context: Refresh is already interceptor-owned with single-flight and an explicit failure path. Whether to move refresh entirely server-side (which would tie into the storage decision above) is a maintainer call.

judgment_calls.question: Is a provider swap on the roadmap (in the next 12–24 months), or is Auth0 locked in for defensive/compliance reasons?
judgment_calls.context: The adapter localization means a swap is cheap mechanically, but the value of doing the work depends on how likely a swap actually is. If Auth0 is locked in, no action is needed; if a swap is realistic, the current shape is what you'd hope to be starting from.

judgment_calls.question: Are authorization model changes planned — finer permissions (RBAC via Auth0 API RBAC, ABAC), Organizations, or a shift to server-issued permission claims — that would extend the current role-based policy?
judgment_calls.context: The current policy is role-string based (admin, billing-admin) with an action map. Moving to permission-scoped or organization-scoped decisions is straightforward inside policy.ts + Principal, but only worth doing if it's actually planned.

judgment_calls.question: MemoryCache in production: is this fixture-grade code representative of the intended production store, or a placeholder to be replaced before shipping?
judgment_calls.context: In real deployments, in-memory token storage evaporates on tab close and provides no isolation from XSS in the same origin. The seam is right; the destination might not be.

synthesis.posture: well-bounded across all four axes and B1–B3; B4 not_applicable (pure SPA)

headline.text: Auth0 v2 is well-bounded here: the SDK import lives in one adapter file, a custom ICache holds token storage, refresh is interceptor-owned with single-flight, and API calls carry the access token (audience configured, so the opaque-token / ID-token-for-API anti-pattern is structurally unreachable) — every mechanical seam the methodology asks for is present. The one item worth naming without maintainer input: MemoryCache is fixture-grade in-memory storage; the seam to swap it exists but the intended production ICache (HttpOnly-cookie-backed, encrypted, etc.) is not yet written.
